newsitem.title: USA: Stocks up for second day as dollar hits four-year high.
newsitem.headline: Stocks up for second day as dollar hits four-year high.

text.p: Stocks' rebounded for a second consecutive session Monday, lifted by a drop in long-term interest rates and a surge in the dollar to a four-year high against the Japanese yen.

The 30-year Treasury bond joined the march upward. So did oil and wheat prices, which soared after a powerful spring snowstorm in the northern Plains knocked out pumping stations and flooded fields slated to be planted soon with spring crops.

The Dow Jones industrial average finished up 29.84 points, or 0.46 percent, at 6,555.91. Monday's rise followed a 49-point advance Friday, which closed a week in which the blue chip average shed more than 214 points.
"Most of the world has been waiting and looking for some kind of a bounce, and this appears to be it," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates.
In the broader market, advances beat declines 1,714 to 771 on active volume of 453 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The Dow's rebound has failed to impress many Wall Street analysts. They cautioned that stocks could come under renewed pressure if long-term interest rates move higher or first-quarter corporate profit reports fail to meet expectations.
Strength in the bond market, where investors reacted to the dollar's rise against foreign currencies, led to bargain hunting and short-covering in stocks, analysts said.

The 30-year Treasury bond was up 20/32 in late trading, or $6.25 on a $1,000 bond, and its yield dropped to 7.07 percent from 7.12 percent Friday. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.
The recovery in stocks was led by technology shares, which were also at the forefront of the broader market's sell-off after they peaked in late January.
The Nasdaq composite, a barometer of the technology sector, had its third consecutive double-digit rise, jumping 14.62, or 1.18 percent, to 1,251.35.
Analysts said investors appeared to be buying technology stocks in anticipation of Motorola Inc.'s first-quarter earnings report. Motorola gained 50 cents to end at $60.25.

After trading closed, Motorola reported first-quarter profits of $325 million, or 53 cents a share, vs. $384 million, or 63 cents, in the year-ago period. But the results beat Wall Street analysts' forecasts.

The Motorola numbers were viewed as the first key piece of earnings news for Wall Street. Concerns that a slowing economy and the stronger dollar will hurt corporate profits have been factors in the recent sell-off.
The dollar rose against the yen as fears the United States would use a weaker dollar to remedy trade imbalances with Japan subsided.

Although Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin urged Japan to guard against widening trade surpluses, his relatively benign rhetoric after meeting Friday with Japanese officials in Tokyo stoked dollar bulls, who had feared he would threaten to use a weaker dollar as a weapon against rising Japanese exports.

The dollar vaulted to above 125 yen Monday, touching 125.81, its highest since January 1993. It settled at 125.58 yen, up from 124.30 late Friday. The dollar rose to 1.7125 German marks from 1.6858 Friday.

In commodity markets, crude oil for May delivery ended 11 cents a barrel higher at $19.23 at the New York Mercantile Exchange. May gasoline ended up 0.24 cent at 60.72 cents a gallon, while May heating oil finished off 0.02 cent a gallon at 53.12 cents.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery closed 8-3/4 cents higher at $3.80-1/2 a bushel.
Overseas, the FTSE 100 closed 35.1 points up at 4,271.7. Tokyo's Nikkei average fell 144.92 points, or 0.81 percent, to 17,715.67.
